lessons.title: The West Coast offense
lessons.objective: You can say what a West Coast offense actually asks the quarterback to do.

payload.prompt: What is the core idea of the West Coast offense?

options.text: Run the ball relentlessly to set up play-action
Use short, quick passes as the running game instead of handing off
Throw the deep ball on every play to stretch the defense

explanation.correct: The West Coast offense treats short passes like runs. The quarterback gets the ball out fast on timing routes, and the receiver runs after the catch. It is a passing system that moves the ball in short chunks like the ground game.
explanation.incorrect: Bill Walsh designed the West Coast to replace runs with fast, precise short passes. The running back catches a slant, a screen, or a checkdown and runs upfield.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That quarterback has West Coast genetics. Ball is out in 2.5 seconds every play.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: A quarterback who was born on the West Coast
A quarterback trained to release the ball very fast on short routes
A quarterback who only plays in the NFL Western Conference
A quarterback who was drafted by a West Coast team

payload.translation: West Coast genetics means the system teaches quarterbacks to get the ball to receivers on time, before coverage has time to tighten. A 2.5-second release is the goal, not the exception.

followUps.line: Why would a quick release matter in a West Coast system?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand that timing routes need precise, fast throws.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: West Coast football is about timing and precision. The receiver breaks at exactly the moment the ball arrives. That only works if the quarterback releases early and on schedule.

payload.prompt: In the West Coast offense, what happens if the primary receiver is covered?

options.text: The quarterback holds the ball and waits for someone to get open
The quarterback goes to the second or third read, often a checkdown to the running back
The quarterback runs with the ball

explanation.correct: The West Coast system gives the quarterback a quick progression: first read, second read, third read, and checkdown. If the first option is covered, he moves fast to the next one. The checkdown is a safety valve.
explanation.incorrect: West Coast quarterbacks work through progressions quickly. They go from their first option to their second to their third, and if all are covered, they check down to the running back for a short gain.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Our offense is just West Coast short stuff today. No one is getting deep.

payload.question: What is he saying about the game plan?

options.text: The team is from the West Coast and plays short games
The quarterback is only throwing to receivers close to the line of scrimmage
The team is playing without its star receiver
The game is in a short stadium

payload.translation: When a coach says West Coast short stuff, he means they are sticking to quick passes, slants, outs and screens. Depth routes are not happening that day, maybe because the defense is aggressive or the coverage is locked down deep.

followUps.line: Would a West Coast coach ever throw deep?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know West Coast is a strategy, not a rule against vertical plays.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: West Coast is a philosophy, not a straight-jacket. Deep routes exist in the system, but the default is fast, short stuff that works on timing.

payload.prompt: Match the West Coast term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A route where the receiver and quarterback work on the same clock. The ball arrives when the receiver breaks, not after.
A short, safe throw to the running back when the primary reads are covered, keeping the play alive.
The order of receivers the quarterback reads pre-snap: first, second, third, and checkdown.

explanation.summary: Timing routes are the heart of West Coast. Progressions tell the quarterback where to look. Checkdowns are the safety net.

lessons.title: Air Raid and spread
lessons.objective: You can spot Air Raid habits.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Five wide, no huddle, this is pure Air Raid. They are going to throw it 50 times.

payload.question: What is she identifying?

options.text: The team is about to pass the ball a lot based on the formation and tempo
The team is literally going to throw the ball exactly 50 times
This is the West Coast offense
The team is in trouble and desperate

payload.translation: Five wide receivers and no huddle are the telltale signs of Air Raid. The system spreads the defense thin with multiple receivers and speeds up the tempo with the no-huddle. A high pass volume is the natural result.

followUps.line: Why would no-huddle help a spread offense?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know that no-huddle limits the defense's ability to substitute and adjust.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Air Raid is more about spreading the field and speeding the game than throwing 50 times. But the formation and tempo do lead to a lot of passes.

payload.prompt: Match the Air Raid term to what it does.

pairs.definition: Four or five receivers spread to the sidelines, leaving the middle empty. It stretches the defense horizontally.
Lining up and snapping without a huddle to force the defense into base packages and stop them from substituting.
Air Raid keeps throwing the same easy read over and over. Simple > complex.

explanation.summary: Spread spreads the field. No-huddle speeds the tempo and limits adjustments. Simple plays repeated work because the defense cannot get set.

payload.prompt: Why does Air Raid use mostly simple, easy reads?

options.text: Because it is a college-only offense
Because the quarterback does not need to be elite to execute them and the repeats create separation
Because defenses cannot figure out simple plays

explanation.correct: Air Raid philosophy says simple is powerful. A slant route run 20 times in different ways beats a complex concept run once. The quarterback does not need a cannon arm or a genius mind, just timing and the same read every time.
explanation.incorrect: Air Raid is designed around easy concepts that can be repeated and adjusted. A simple slant with motion can beat almost any defense if the receiver and quarterback are on time.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: No-huddle, hurry-up. They are gassing the defense and forcing a nickel package.

payload.question: Why is Air Raid trying to gas the defense?

options.text: To tire out the players before the playoffs
To keep the defense from substituting and force them into an ill-equipped package
To get the crowd excited
Because the offense has no other strategy

payload.translation: When Air Raid speeds up the tempo and forces the defense to stay on the field with nickels in (five defensive backs), the defense loses its run-stopping strength. That is the trap: the fast pace prevents adjustment and puts mismatches on the field.

followUps.line: What does nickel package mean for the defense?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know nickel is more pass-focused and weaker against the run.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Air Raid tempo is not random energy. It is a weapon to force the defense into specific packages that cannot do everything.

lessons.title: Outside zone and play-action
lessons.objective: You can explain why one play sells the other.

payload.prompt: Put the Shanahan scheme flow in the right order.

items.text: Read the edge of the play and stretch it laterally
items.why: Outside zone is a run where the back stretches the ball sideways to find a lane, then cuts upfield.

items.text: Plant and cut back inside off a puller or free lane
items.why: After feeling for the edge, the back finds a crease and cuts back. This is where the yards come.

items.text: Fake the same outside-zone look with play-action
items.why: Now the defense is keying on that outside-zone stretch. Play-action uses the same fake to freeze linebackers.

items.text: Throw vertical off the play-action fake
items.why: While linebackers crash trying to stop the run, receivers run vertical routes. The window opens behind them.

explanation.correct: The Shanahan offense runs outside zone, the linebackers bite on the run fake, then play-action freezes them. Vertical routes turn into big plays because the linebackers are out of position.
explanation.incorrect: Outside zone sets up play-action by making the run look real. When the linebacker reacts to the stretch, the fake handoff and bootleg turn him inside-out.

payload.prompt: Why is play-action so effective right after outside zone runs?

options.text: Because the defense is tired
Because linebackers are keyed on the outside-zone stretch and chase it before the fake works
Because the quarterback is a better thrower than runner

explanation.correct: Outside zone trains linebackers to react to the stretch and flow laterally. When play-action uses the same fake, they bite hard. By the time they realize it is a pass, the back has a free run up the middle or the receiver is running vertical.
explanation.incorrect: The Shanahan system is built on respect. Run the ball enough outside, and the defense has to flow with it. Play-action punishes that instinct with a quick pass or bootleg.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: That is how the bootleg works. The end crashed on the outside-zone fake, so the quarterback has a mile of space.

payload.question: What did the bootleg accomplish?

options.text: It confused the quarterback
It used the run fake to get the defensive end to chase the wrong way and open space for a pass or scramble
It replaced the running back on the play
It made the defense too tired to stop the next play

payload.translation: A bootleg in the Shanahan scheme uses the outside-zone look to suck in the defensive end. The quarterback goes the other way on a run-pass option or a designed bootleg, and the end is too far upfield to pursue.

followUps.line: Why does the outside-zone run set up a bootleg better than an inside-zone run?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know that outside zone pulls the defense wider.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Shanahan football is about using run fakes to displace defenders. The bootleg gets the edge rusher going the wrong way, leaving grass the other way.

payload.prompt: What does the Shanahan offense need to make outside zone work?

options.text: The defense has to respect the run game enough to pursue it laterally
A very fast running back
The smartest quarterback in the league

explanation.correct: Outside zone works because the defense reacts to the stretch. If the defense stays home and shoots gaps, the run dies. But the Shanahan system has run it enough that defenses feel obligated to flow with the ball. Respect for the run is what kills it on play-action.
explanation.incorrect: Outside zone is not about having the fastest running back. It is about creating a lane through downhill cuts and blocks. The running back reads one step and plants. Defense has to respect the run, or it wins.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: That is zone blocking. The guards are working together, and the back is reading the hole, not following a lead blocker.

payload.question: How is zone blocking different from what he was describing?

options.text: Zone blocking assigns players to gaps; the back finds the hole. Gap blocking assigns each player a target.
Zone blocking only works in college
Zone blocking is when everyone blocks the same defender
Zone blocking prevents holding penalties

payload.translation: Zone blocking is the Shanahan staple. The O-line does not follow one guy; they block an area or level. The back reads which blocker has the advantage and cuts there. This is why outside zone can bounce to the edge or cut back inside.

followUps.line: Why does zone blocking give the back more options than gap blocking?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know zone creates flexibility for the runner.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Zone blocking is just linemen saying, 'I have this area,' and the back picking the best lane. It is simpler than calling out each man's job.

lessons.title: Motion tells
lessons.objective: You can use motion to guess man or zone.

statement.speaker: Quarterback
statement.text: Before the snap, I motion my receiver across the formation. The corner follows him. That is man coverage.

payload.question: How does the motion tell him it is man?

options.text: In man coverage, a defender shadows one player everywhere he goes
The corner is just being friendly
Motion always reveals coverage
The corner is confused by the motion

payload.translation: When a receiver motions across the formation, he tests the coverage. In man coverage, the defender assigned to him follows. In zone coverage, the defender stays in his zone. The corner following is a dead giveaway that it is man-to-man.

followUps.line: What would happen if it were zone coverage and the receiver motioned?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know the defender would stay in place, not follow.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Motion is a spy tool. Receivers move before the snap and the defense's reaction tells you if it is man or zone. Man defenders follow; zone defenders ignore the motion.

payload.prompt: Why do offenses use motion before the snap?

options.text: To confuse the defense into penalties
To read coverage and find weak spots
Because it is fun to move around

explanation.correct: Motion is intelligence. The quarterback wants to know: is this man or zone? How many are in the box? Motion reveals those answers. A defender following is man. A defender standing still is zone. That changes the read.
explanation.incorrect: Before the snap, offenses motion a receiver or back across the formation. The defense's reaction tells the quarterback what to expect. That determines the play call or the hot route.

statement.speaker: Safety
statement.text: I see the motion and I rotate from a single-high to the boundary to give the corner help deep.

payload.question: What is the safety revealing?

options.text: The safety is confused
It is zone coverage. The safety rotates to help the zone, not because one receiver moved.
The safety is leaving the center of the field open
The defense is about to blitz

payload.translation: When a safety rotates pre-snap in response to alignment or motion, that is a zone tell. In man coverage, the safety does not adjust based on where one receiver lines up; he has his own area. Pre-snap rotations are pure zone.

followUps.line: Would a safety rotate in man coverage?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know man coverage leaves safeties over the top and less flexible.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Zone safeties are adjustable. They move to cover vulnerable areas. Man coverage safeties are over-the-top help and do not move much. Watch the safety's pre-snap movement to know which it is.

payload.prompt: What else can motion reveal besides man or zone?

options.text: How many defenders are in the box, which tells you if the defense is ready to stop the run
The color of the defense's jerseys
Whether the defense is happy or sad

explanation.correct: Motion can tell the quarterback how many defenders are near the line of scrimmage. If the defense keeps everyone home, the box stays full. If they pull a linebacker to follow the motion, the box gets light. Light box means run the ball. Full box means pass.
explanation.incorrect: By motioning a running back to the slot and watching the response, the quarterback sees if a linebacker follows. If one does, the box count drops by one. That changes play calls.

lessons.title: Match and disguise
lessons.objective: You can explain why coverage names are slippery.

options.text: A coverage that starts like zone but turns into man once receivers enter the coverage area
A coverage where everyone plays man coverage
A coverage where everyone plays zone coverage

explanation.correct: Match coverage is hybrid. Pre-snap it looks like a zone, so the offense has a hard time reading it. Post-snap, once a receiver enters the zone area, that zone defender takes the man. It is zone until a man enters it, then it switches. Hard to see and hard to beat.
explanation.incorrect: Modern defenses do not stay pure. Match coverage lets them start in a zone look but function like man once routes develop. A linebacker drops in zone until a running back enters his area, then he covers the back man-to-man.

payload.prompt: You are the defense. Call match coverage and disguise it as Cover 2. What do you gain?

situation.narrative: The offense is running a route combination designed to beat Cover 2. You want to show them Cover 2 pre-snap, but you have match coverage that can adjust when routes develop.

facts.label: Offensive read
facts.value: Routes designed to hit seams in Cover 2

facts.label: Advantage
facts.value: If they react to the Cover 2 look, they run into your match coverage

options.label: Disguise match as Cover 2 and let them run into it
options.consequence: The offense sees two safeties and throws to the seam. But your zone defender has already matched the tight end or running back man-to-man. The throw is incomplete or intercepted.
considerations: They see Cover 2 but get something else

options.label: Just play pure Cover 2
options.consequence: You show what you are. The offense runs the exact seam route designed to beat Cover 2. They complete it and gain 15 yards.
considerations: Disguise is worth more than honesty

payload.expertNote: Modern defenses win with disguise. Showing one coverage and playing another lets the defense react to what happens, not just what the offense planned.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: They called Cover 2 but they disguised it as Cover 3. Post-snap, a linebacker matched the running back.

payload.question: Why is the coverage name confusing?

options.text: The analyst is wrong about what coverage it was
Modern defenses mix and match so much that the name becomes slippery and depends on post-snap action
Cover 2 and Cover 3 are the same thing
The defense is breaking the rules

payload.translation: Coverage names come from the safeties and how they align pre-snap. But match and hybrid coverages blur the lines. A coverage is called Cover 2, but it becomes something else once a receiver enters an area. That is why announcers sometimes disagree on what coverage it is.

followUps.line: Is it still Cover 2 if it changes after the snap?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know coverage is fluid, not fixed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Coverage names are based on what you see pre-snap. But modern defenses rotate and match post-snap. The name might not fit the execution. That is by design.

payload.prompt: Why do defenses use hybrid match coverages instead of pure man or pure zone?

options.text: Because it confuses the offense and lets the defense adapt to what happens on the field
Because pure coverage is illegal
Because players are too stupid to learn pure coverage

explanation.correct: Hybrid coverage gives defenses the best of both worlds. Zone foundation = hard to read pre-snap. Man rules post-snap = adaptable to what routes do. The offense cannot key on one thing because the defense might be doing two things at once.
explanation.incorrect: Modern defenses have learned that you do not have to be pure. Start in a zone look to hide your intentions, then switch to man once routes develop. The quarterback sees zone pre-snap but faces man coverage post-snap.

lessons.title: Tampa 2 and zone blitz
lessons.objective: You can describe two classic defensive ideas.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept to what it does.

pairs.definition: A Cover 2 where the middle linebacker drops back deep to cover the hole between the safeties, creating a three-deep look.
A blitz where a lineman drops into coverage while a linebacker or safety rushes, confusing blocking assignments.
The unpredictability created when you do not rush your front four and mix who attacks versus who covers.

explanation.summary: Tampa 2 is a secondary coverage. Zone blitz is a pass rush concept. Both hide what the defense is doing until after the snap.

options.text: Because it was invented in Tampa by the Buccaneers in the 1990s
Because it has two safeties deep
Because there are two Tampas in Florida

explanation.correct: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers and defensive coordinator Monte Kiffin popularized this coverage in the mid-1990s. It stopped the vertical pass with the Mike linebacker dropping deep. The name stuck because the team won a Super Bowl with it.
explanation.incorrect: Tampa 2 comes from Tampa Bay, where the Bucs used it to dominate. It is a Cover 2 with the middle linebacker dropping to the hole, creating three deep defenders against vertical throws.

statement.speaker: Offensive Coordinator
statement.text: They are showing a four-man rush but it is a zone blitz. The end is dropping, and the linebacker is coming up the middle.

payload.question: Why is this deception a problem?

options.text: The offensive line is expecting a four-man rush from the line and gets fooled when a linebacker comes free
The zone blitz is illegal
The offense cannot run the ball on this play
The quarterback is required to throw the ball instantly

payload.translation: Zone blitz is a misdirection. The line blocks the four guys they see, but one of them is dropping back. Meanwhile, a linebacker or safety comes up the middle or the edge unblocked. The free rusher is devastating because nobody planned to stop him.

followUps.line: How would the offense stop a free rusher from a zone blitz?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know the offense needs a hot route or check to pick up the unblocked rusher.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Zone blitz wins because it creates a free rusher from misdirection, not extra bodies. That unpredictability is worth more than numbers.

payload.prompt: How is Tampa 2 coverage different from regular Cover 2?

options.text: The middle linebacker drops deep to protect the seams, adding a third level of coverage
The corners play closer to the receivers
There are three safeties instead of two

explanation.correct: Standard Cover 2 has two safeties at the top covering two-thirds of the field and corners on the outside. Tampa 2 adds a third layer: the Mike linebacker drops back to cover the middle seam where a tight end or slot might run vertical. Three deep, two cornerbacks. Very hard to complete seam routes.
explanation.incorrect: Tampa 2 is Cover 2 with the middle linebacker dropping into the middle of the field post-snap. That third deep defender stops dig routes and seam routes cold, but it weakens run defense because the Mike is back in coverage.

lessons.title: Boxes and mismatches
lessons.objective: You can say why the box count and mismatches drive play calls.

payload.prompt: The defense is in a single-high shell. You count six defenders in the box. Run or pass?

situation.narrative: It is second and eight. One safety is deep. Six defenders are near the line of scrimmage to stop the run.

facts.label: Threat
facts.value: The safety is one-on-one against a receiver

options.label: Run the ball
options.consequence: Six defenders can stop six blockers. There is no crease. You get three yards and face third and long.
considerations: But six is not light enough
You need a mismatch or open field

options.label: Throw it to a receiver
options.consequence: The safety is alone over the top. A receiver running vertical has a one-on-one chance. Gain eight or more and move the chains.
considerations: Box count is not the only read

payload.expertNote: Box count drives run calls, and coverage shell drives pass calls. A light box invites runs, but a single-high shell invites vertical shots. In tension, trust the shell.

statement.speaker: Quarterback
statement.text: Their linebacker is covering our slot receiver. That is a mismatch. We are going to abuse that all day.

payload.question: Why does he want to throw to the slot?

options.text: The linebacker is bigger and will fall down
The receiver is faster and more agile than the linebacker, creating an advantage
Slot receivers always beat linebackers
The quarterback is tired of running plays

payload.translation: A mismatch is when a receiver faces a defender who is not built to cover him. Fast tight end on a linebacker. Slot receiver on a safety. The natural weapons do not match the responsibility. The quarterback attacks it.

followUps.line: How does a defense create the mismatch it wants the offense to attack?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know defenses sometimes invite bad matchups to get rush pressure.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Mismatch is about fit, not talent. A linebacker on a slot is a mismatch because the linebacker is not trained to cover that space. The defense is trying to blitz and leaving a weak spot.

payload.prompt: What does a quarterback read when he counts the box?

options.text: Whether the defense can stop the run, which helps him choose between run and pass
How much the defense loves him
What the weather is going to be

explanation.correct: The quarterback counts defenders inside the box (roughly from tackle to tackle, near the line). Seven or more = full box = good run. Six or fewer = light box = pass all day. It is math: if you have more blockers than defenders, run it. If defenders outnumber, throw it.
explanation.incorrect: Box count is a pre-snap read. Eight defenders in the box and five receivers? You are outnumbered, better pass. Six in the box and five blockers? You have numbers, hand it off.

statement.speaker: Safety
statement.text: We are in a single-high shell. I am one-on-one with their number-one receiver. Best of luck to me.

payload.question: What is the safety worried about?

options.text: The defense has no help over the top so he is vulnerable to deep throws
The weather is bad
The receiver is shorter than him
The field is wet

payload.translation: Single-high means one safety deep and no help. The corners and receivers are on islands. A deep pass to a great receiver in one-on-one coverage is a coin flip. The offense likes this, especially with speed or height advantages.

followUps.line: Why would a defense show single-high if it is so dangerous?
followUps.why: Tests whether you know defenses sacrifice some coverage to stop the run.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Single-high is a gamble. You get better run defense and less yardage to the first down, but you lose deep safety help. One-on-one corners can lose. Elite receivers win that coin flip.
